# **Exhaustive Analysis of the DIQA-5000 Dataset and Submissions to the VQualA 2025 Document Image Quality Assessment Challenge**

## **The Paradigm Shift in Document Image Quality Assessment**

The ubiquitous proliferation of digital mobile technologies has fundamentally restructured the mechanisms through which information is stored, processed, and transmitted globally.1 Despite the rapid transition toward paperless administrative and corporate environments, the digitization of physical paper documents remains an indispensable operational requirement across legal, academic, medical, and governmental sectors. High-quality digital scans serve as the critical bridge for seamless integration between physical artifacts and digital archival systems.1 However, the modern digitization pipeline has increasingly shifted away from controlled, high-fidelity flatbed scanners toward consumer-grade mobile smartphone cameras.2 This transition introduces profound environmental and technical variables. Variations in capture devices, unpredictable ambient illumination, and inconsistent user handling frequently result in severe degradations of document image quality, necessitating robust, algorithmically driven document enhancement techniques.1

The evaluation of these enhancement techniques presents a unique challenge that diverges significantly from traditional image processing paradigms. In the realm of natural images, quality is predominantly judged through the lens of aesthetic appeal, color harmony, and visual pleasantness. Conversely, the intrinsic value of a document image is inextricably bound to its structural integrity, textual legibility, and functional utility.2 A photograph of a natural landscape may retain its aesthetic value even when subjected to minor motion blur or sensor noise; however, a document suffering from identical distortions may experience catastrophic failure when processed by Optical Character Recognition (OCR) systems.1 Consequently, Document Image Quality Assessment (DIQA) has evolved into a highly specialized, mission-critical subfield of computer vision. DIQA serves as the foundational mechanism for evaluating the efficacy of document restoration algorithms, optimizing automated OCR processing pipelines, and ensuring the reliability of digital record-keeping.1

Historically, the evaluation of document quality relied upon indirect, downstream surrogate metrics—most notably, the character error rate (CER) generated by an OCR engine—or generalized, full-reference image quality assessment (IQA) algorithms such as Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and the Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM).3 These legacy approaches exhibit severe methodological limitations. Hand-crafted feature extraction and shallow convolutional models often fail to capture the high-level semantic layout and structural dependencies required to holistically evaluate a text-heavy image.4 Furthermore, full-reference metrics demand a pristine, uncorrupted "ground truth" image for pixel-by-pixel comparison, a luxury that is virtually non-existent in authentic mobile capture scenarios.3 To overcome these fundamental barriers, the research community has pivoted toward the development of no-reference (blind) DIQA models powered by deep neural networks, which are designed to correlate computational quality predictions directly with subjective human perceptual judgments.3

It is within this transitional scientific landscape that the DIQA-5000 dataset was engineered. As the demand for sophisticated document restoration algorithms (such as geometric dewarping, shadow removal, and deblurring) accelerated, the absence of a standardized, large-scale framework to objectively evaluate their perceptual quality became a critical bottleneck.5 The DIQA-5000 dataset was conceptualized to resolve this deficiency, providing an exhaustive, multidimensional benchmark to train, validate, and evaluate the next generation of human-aligned perceptual document quality assessment models.1

## **Architectural Topography of the DIQA-5000 Benchmark Dataset**

The DIQA-5000 dataset represents a foundational leap in the objective, quantitative evaluation of document image enhancement techniques. Prior to its introduction, researchers attempting to gauge the efficacy of document restoration algorithms were forced to rely on fragmented, small-scale datasets, or datasets entirely optimized for binary OCR accuracy rather than human perceptual comfort.5 The architecture of the DIQA-5000 dataset was meticulously designed to encompass the vast spectrum of degradations and semantic variations encountered in the wild.

The genesis of the dataset relies upon a carefully curated source corpus of 500 original document images, all of which were captured natively using consumer mobile phones.2 To guarantee exceptional ecological validity and ensure that models trained on this data do not overfit to a specific structural template, the source documents span a highly diverse array of content categories. The corpus encompasses dense text-heavy academic pages, complex tabular financial data, scientific diagrams, handwritten administrative notes, and highly unstructured mixed-layout forms.5 The linguistic and symbolic representation within the dataset is equally diverse, featuring continuous English prose, dense Chinese character structures, and intricate mathematical symbology.5

To accurately simulate the hostile capture conditions frequently encountered by mobile users, the original 500 source documents were subjected to a battery of natural and synthetic degradations.2 The dataset encapsulates five primary distortion topologies. Shadows and uneven illumination profiles simulate the occlusion of ambient light sources by the user's hand, body, or the mobile device itself during capture. Physical occlusions mimic foreign objects resting on the document surface. Defocus and motion blur artifacts represent the camera shake and improper focal length adjustments endemic to rapid, handheld mobile photography. Creases and geometric warping capture the nonlinear distortions caused by the physical folding, crumpling, or curved resting state of bound paper documents. Finally, moiré patterns introduce the high-frequency interference artifacts generated when capturing images of documents displayed on liquid crystal or light-emitting diode screens.2

Following the degradation phase, the dataset creators applied a sophisticated matrix of document enhancement algorithms to generate the final image corpus.1 Six distinct, state-of-the-art enhancement functions were utilized: geometric dewarping to correct nonlinear physical folds, demoiréing to suppress frequency interference, occlusion removal, image deblurring, deshadowing, and general contrast and appearance enhancement.2 By applying diverse, randomized combinations of these algorithmic corrections, the researchers generated 10 distinct enhanced versions for each of the 500 original degraded documents, yielding the final robust dataset of 5,000 enhanced document images.2

### **Multidimensional Psychometric Annotation Protocols**

The most critical differentiator of the DIQA-5000 dataset, elevating it above legacy benchmarks, is its reliance on exhaustive, multidimensional human perceptual annotations.1 The dataset creators recognized that the concept of document quality cannot be mathematically distilled into a single, monolithic scalar value without sacrificing critical diagnostic information. For instance, an image may possess excellent color accuracy but suffer from catastrophic structural warping, rendering it unreadable. To capture these nuances, the DIQA-5000 dataset provides continuous Mean Opinion Scores (MOS) across three distinct, orthogonal rating dimensions 2:

1. **Overall Quality:** A holistic, subjective assessment of the document's total utility, readability, and visual clarity.  
2. **Sharpness:** A targeted evaluation of high-frequency textual edges, structural definition, and the suppression of algorithmic blurring artifacts.  
3. **Color Fidelity:** The perceptual accuracy of the background chromaticity and foreground ink representations relative to the physical artifact, specifically penalizing color shifting induced by aggressive deshadowing algorithms.

The annotation protocol adhered to stringent international psychometric standards to guarantee reproducibility. The evaluation utilized a pairwise comparison methodology, wherein human annotators viewed the original degraded document image and the algorithmically enhanced image side-by-side in a controlled viewing environment.5 A panel of 15 highly trained annotators, specifically selected for their domain expertise in document processing and digital archival, evaluated every image in the dataset.5 To guarantee maximum statistical reliability and to mathematically mitigate the impact of subjective rater fatigue or idiosyncratic bias, outlier scores were systematically identified and discarded in strict accordance with the ITU-R BT.500 recommendations.3

### **The Distributional Variance Constraint**

While the DIQA-5000 dataset provides highly accurate Mean Opinion Scores for each of the 5,000 document images, it features a critical architectural constraint: the dataset omits the standard deviation (variance) of the human annotations across the panel of raters.4 In contemporary Image Quality Assessment research, particularly when training Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), continuous quality scores are rarely treated as absolute scalars. Instead, they are modeled as continuous Gaussian distributions, denoted as ![][image1], where ![][image2] represents the Mean Opinion Score and ![][image3] represents the variance.4 This distributional modeling is mathematically required to convert continuous numerical scalars into discrete probability tokens (e.g., classifying a score as 60% "good" and 40% "excellent"), which MLLMs require to calculate cross-entropy loss during backpropagation.4

The total absence of ground-truth variance annotations in the DIQA-5000 dataset presented a profound structural barrier for researchers attempting to map continuous MOS values to discrete textual labels. This specific constraint compelled participating researchers to engineer highly novel mathematical workarounds—most notably pseudo-variance injection and linear interpolation mapping—which ultimately became the defining architectural characteristics of the most successful methodologies deployed against the dataset.4

## **Ecosystem of Competitions Utilizing the DIQA-5000 Dataset**

An exhaustive review of the available research literature and competition platforms indicates that the DIQA-5000 dataset was developed explicitly for, and utilized exclusively by, the **VQualA 2025 Document Image Quality Assessment Challenge**.2 While the VQualA 2025 event hosted multiple concurrent challenges focused on diverse visual domains, the DIQA track served as the premier, singular benchmarking arena for this newly minted document corpus.

The VQualA (Visual Quality Assessment Competition) Workshop, hosted in conjunction with the prestigious IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV) 2025, represents a concentrated global effort to advance perceptual quality evaluation in computer vision.2 The workshop explicitly targets the known limitations of traditional, structurally rigid metrics like PSNR and SSIM, leveraging recent breakthroughs in deep learning, generative diffusion models, and Multimodal Large Language Models to foster human-aligned computational assessments.9

To fully contextualize the scope of the VQualA 2025 summit, it is necessary to note the seven parallel challenges hosted under its umbrella, each targeting a specific sub-domain of visual quality 8:

1. **ISRGC-Q:** Image Super-Resolution Generated Content Quality Assessment Challenge, utilizing the ISRGen-QA dataset.8  
2. **FIQA:** Face Image Quality Assessment Challenge, targeting biometric and perceptual face degradations in the wild.8  
3. **EVQA-SnapUGC:** Engagement Prediction for Short Videos Challenge, correlating video quality with user retention metrics.8  
4. **Visual Quality Comparison for LMMs:** A challenge requiring Large Multimodal Models to perform open-ended reasoning regarding visual differences, utilizing the Co-Instruct-562K dataset.8  
5. **GenAI-Bench AIGC Video Quality Assessment (Track I and Track II):** Challenges focused on evaluating the temporal and spatial quality of AI-generated video content.8  
6. **DIQA:** Document Image Quality Assessment Challenge, serving as the exclusive proving ground for the DIQA-5000 dataset.8

The DIQA track was uniquely organized through a collaborative effort between Shanghai Jiao Tong University, INTSIG Information Co. Ltd, and the broader VQualA 2025 committee.5 The primary mandate of the competition was to catalyze the development of perceptual quality assessment models that exhibit a Pearson correlation nearing 1.0 with human judgment, thereby enabling the rapid, automated benchmarking of enhancement algorithms in practical industrial pipelines.5

## **Mechanics and Evaluation Protocols of the VQualA 2025 DIQA Challenge**

The VQualA 2025 DIQA Challenge operated on a highly structured timeline hosted on the CodaLab platform, designed to facilitate rigorous machine learning practices and prevent data leakage.5 The competition commenced with the development phase on May 24, 2025, triggering the release of the training and validation subsets of the DIQA-5000 dataset to registered participants.5 The final testing phase was executed in a tightly controlled window from July 1, 2025, to July 4, 2025, culminating in the submission of technique reports and fact sheets by July 11, 2025\.5

The challenge generated significant global academic and industrial interest. Official statistics reveal that 120 individual participants registered for the DIQA track.2 Throughout the competition's lifecycle, the participants organized into 16 mutually exclusive, distinct teams.2 During the development phase, these 16 teams submitted a total of 183 preliminary prediction results to the validation server to receive immediate correlational feedback.2 Following the release of the blinded testing data, the 16 participating teams submitted a total of 97 final prediction arrays.2 However, to be officially ranked on the final leaderboard and become eligible for academic publication, teams were strictly required to submit fully executable source code reproducing their results, alongside detailed technical fact sheets outlining their algorithmic architectures.2 Ultimately, 7 teams successfully completed this rigorous verification protocol, representing the definitive submissions to the DIQA-5000 dataset.2

### **Dataset Partitioning Strategy**

To guarantee the scientific integrity of the submitted models, the DIQA-5000 dataset was strictly partitioned. The organizers implemented a crucial constraint: all 10 enhanced versions of any single original source document were mathematically forced into the same subset.2 This prevented algorithms from memorizing the underlying semantic structure of a document in the training set and artificially inflating their performance when encountering a differently enhanced version of the same document in the testing set.2

| Dataset Partition | Total Images | Percentage | Original Source Documents | Annotation Data Provided |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Training Set** | 3,500 | 70% | 350 | Full MOS (Overall, Sharpness, Color) |
| **Validation Set** | 500 | 10% | 50 | Full MOS (Overall, Sharpness, Color) |
| **Testing Set** | 1,000 | 20% | 100 | Blinded (Input Images Only) |

### **Mathematical Evaluation Framework**

To determine the hierarchy of the leaderboard, the VQualA 2025 organizers instituted a dual-metric evaluation protocol designed to measure both the absolute numerical accuracy and the relative ranking consistency of the predicted quality scores against the human Mean Opinion Scores.2

The first metric utilized was the **Pearson Linear Correlation Coefficient (PLCC)**. The PLCC serves as a strict measure of prediction accuracy, evaluating how closely the model's scalar outputs align with the human labels in a linear space.2 Recognizing that neural networks often output values in disparate dynamic ranges, the organizers required the application of a third-order polynomial nonlinear regression to the model's predictions prior to calculating the PLCC, ensuring a mathematically fair alignment of the score distributions.2

The second metric utilized was the **Spearman Rank-Order Correlation Coefficient (SROCC)**. The SROCC evaluates the monotonic consistency of the model.2 This metric is highly critical in practical deployment scenarios, as it measures whether the algorithm correctly orders a batch of images from lowest to highest quality, completely irrespective of the absolute scalar values assigned to them.2

For each of the three perceptual dimensions (Overall Quality, Sharpness, and Color Fidelity), an intermediate dimensional score was computed by equally weighting the PLCC and SROCC metrics.5 The final placement on the official leaderboard was dictated by a composite Main Score. The Main Score heavily weighted the holistic, overall utility of the document image, while assigning equal, subsidiary weight to the specific optical properties of sharpness and color rendering.2

### **Baseline Model Performance Deficits**

To establish a comparative scientific benchmark and underscore the necessity of the DIQA-5000 dataset, the challenge organizers independently evaluated several state-of-the-art, general-purpose deep learning IQA models against the 1,000 unreleased images in the testing set.2 The selected baseline models represented a comprehensive cross-section of conventional IQA architectures, including older convolutional paradigms like DBCNN, alongside more modern vision transformer networks such as HyperIQA, MUSIQ, StairIQA, TReS, and RichIQA.2

The empirical results of these baseline evaluations illuminated the severe limitations of applying generic natural image metrics directly to document spaces.

| Baseline Model | Architectural Paradigm | Main Score |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **DBCNN** | Convolutional Neural Network | 0.587 |
| **HyperIQA** | Self-Adaptive Network | 0.844 |
| **StairIQA** | Hierarchical Feature Fusion | 0.850 |
| **MUSIQ** | Multi-Scale Image Quality Transformer | 0.859 |
| **TReS** | Transformer-based Relative Ranking | 0.863 |
| **RichIQA** | Advanced Feature Extraction | 0.866 |

The DBCNN model, relying purely on static convolutional filters, achieved a dismal Main Score of 0.587, indicating a near-complete inability to understand the semantic necessity of textual legibility.2 While the more advanced vision transformer architectures performed significantly better—with RichIQA establishing the highest baseline benchmark at 0.866—they universally failed to approach the 0.90 threshold indicative of strong alignment with human perception.2 This stark performance gap highlighted that generalized IQA models cannot inherently differentiate between aesthetically pleasing natural textures and structurally vital character edges, validating the necessity for the specialized algorithms developed during the challenge.2

## **Exhaustive Review of Verified Team Submissions**

The seven teams that successfully submitted reproducible source code and detailed technical fact sheets deployed a vast array of cutting-edge neural network architectures. The most successful approaches universally abandoned pure Convolutional Neural Networks, treating document quality assessment not merely as a localized pixel-regression task, but as a complex, high-level visual-linguistic reasoning problem. The following is a comprehensive analysis of the algorithmic frameworks engineered by all verified teams.

### **1\. Team DeQA-Doc (Rank 1 \- Main Score: 0.929)**

Led by Junjie Gao, Team DeQA-Doc secured the championship by achieving an unprecedented Main Score of 0.929, representing a massive 7.3% correlational improvement over the most advanced baseline model.2 The team's methodology was defined by the successful adaptation of the DeQA-Score framework—a state-of-the-art Multimodal Large Language Model previously utilized exclusively for generic image scoring—into the highly constrained domain of document analysis.4

The central algorithmic innovation of the DeQA-Doc approach was dedicated to solving the "missing variance" conundrum inherent to the DIQA-5000 dataset.4 Because massive MLLMs operate natively on discrete textual tokens rather than continuous numerical regressors, the continuous scalar MOS values had to be mathematically transformed into categorical probability distributions across five distinct linguistic quality levels: {"bad", "poor", "fair", "good", "excellent"}.4 As this transformation typically requires modeling the quality score as a Gaussian distribution ![][image1], the absence of variance (![][image3]) data necessitated the engineering of two rigorous alternatives to construct valid "soft labels" for cross-entropy training.4

First, the team developed a **Pseudo-Variance Injection** mechanism. Relying on empirical statistical meta-analyses of other established IQA datasets (such as KonIQ, SPAQ, and KADID), the researchers determined that the average standard deviation of human scoring typically accounts for approximately 20% of the absolute full scoring range.4 Consequently, they synthesized a dynamic pseudo standard deviation for every DIQA-5000 training sample using the formula ![][image6].4 By normalizing all continuous scores to a rigid $$ scale and scaling the pseudo-variance proportionally, the continuous target data was smoothly distributed across the five discrete textual tokens, enabling stable MLLM gradient descent.4

Second, as a complementary strategy to simulate instances where human variance is assumed to approach zero (functioning mathematically as a unit impulse function), the team utilized a **Linear Interpolation Mapping** schema.12 Given a normalized mean score ![][image2], the algorithm locates the two immediately adjacent discrete level centers ![][image7] and ![][image8]. The probability soft label ![][image9] for any given class ![][image10] is deterministically assigned as ![][image11] for the lower bound class, and ![][image12] for the upper bound class, with all other classes receiving a probability of zero.12 This provided a theoretically sound, lightweight surrogate for full distributional information.12

Leveraging these label-construction methodologies, the team fine-tuned massive foundational MLLMs, initializing weights from **mPLUG-Owl2-7B** and **Qwen2.5-VL-7B**.14 They independently trained specialized network variants for each of the three assessment dimensions (sharpness, color, overall), before aggregating the outputs via an ensemble "DeQA-Mix" aggregator to yield final, highly correlated predictions.14

### **2\. Team mapleyzzzz (Rank 2 \- Main Score: 0.927)**

Operating under the direction of Michael Ao, Team mapleyzzzz secured second place with a Main Score of 0.927.2 Their architectural strategy bypassed reliance on any single network backbone, deploying instead a massive multi-model ensemble framework that synthesized the predictive capabilities of three distinctly fine-tuned MLLMs: **Qwen2.5-VL-7B**, **mPLUG-Owl2-LLaMA2-7B**, and the exceptionally parameter-dense **Qwen2.5-VL-32B**.2

The fundamental methodology of mapleyzzzz mirrored the champions by relying on the precise alignment of visual embeddings with discrete textual templates across a five-level categorical spectrum ({bad, poor, fair, good, perfect}).2 The team explicitly modeled the quality predictions using Gaussian distributions, driving model convergence through Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence loss functions designed to penalize deviations from the human label distributions.2

A defining facet of their approach was the extensive use of cross-modal prompt engineering to construct contextual awareness within the models. For the Qwen2.5-VL variants, the team utilized context-aware textual prompts that actively provided reference points, concatenating images within the prompt structure such as: *"The original image is image1, the processed image is image2. Rate its quality"*.2 Conversely, the mPLUG-Owl2 models within the ensemble were trained utilizing strict pairwise comparison constraints enforced by a distinct fidelity loss function.2 By averaging the softmax probability distributions generated by these three highly diverse models, the team successfully neutralized the individual inductive biases of each architecture, yielding highly robust correlations.

### **3\. Team QA-Veteran (Rank 3 \- Main Score: 0.925)**

Team QA-Veteran, led by Weixia Zhang, achieved a Main Score of 0.925 by engineering a highly specialized framework explicitly designed to combat the destructive nature of standard computer vision preprocessing pipelines.2 The team built their architecture upon the **SigLIP2-NaFlex** vision-language model.2

The core hypothesis driving QA-Veteran was that document images present an unparalleled spatial challenge. A standard mobile document scan frequently exceeds 12 megapixels and contains microscopic, high-frequency textural data essential to legibility. Traditional deep learning pipelines aggressively downsample or square-crop input tensors, which irrevocably destroys the precise optical phenomena (like text sharpness or subtle algorithmic blurring) that DIQA attempts to measure.2 To circumvent this, the team leveraged the **NaFlex** (Native Resolution and Aspect Ratio Flexibility) mechanism native to the SigLIP2 architecture.2 This protocol permitted the model to ingest and process document images at variable, extreme native resolutions while rigidly preserving the original geometric aspect ratio, ensuring that localized artifacts and minute defocus blurs were perfectly preserved within the latent feature space.2

During the inference stage, QA-Veteran utilized a dynamic textual template mechanism.2 They encoded the prompt string: *"a photo with {d} {c} quality"*, where the variable ![][image13] dynamically iterated through the assessment dimensions (![][image14]) and ![][image15] represented the rating levels from 1 to 5\.2 The model extracted the high-resolution visual embedding from the document image and computed the mathematical cosine similarity against the textual embeddings of all possible template variations.2 A softmax function was applied to these discrete similarity scores to derive a continuous probability distribution, which was then scalarized to produce the final continuous prediction metric.2

### **4\. Team NJUST-KMG (Rank 4 \- Main Score: 0.924)**

Led by Zhe Zhang, Team NJUST-KMG achieved a highly competitive Main Score of 0.924 through the implementation of a meticulously crafted training and inference pipeline, characterized by exceptional computational efficiency.2 They employed an ensemble of fine-tuned Multimodal Vision-Language Models, specifically fusing the predictive capabilities of **MiMo-VL-7B-RL**, **Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct**, and **Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct**.2

Rather than executing computationally prohibitive full-parameter fine-tuning on these massive language models, the team elected to freeze the visual encoder backbones entirely.15 They applied Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) modules exclusively to the text decoder layers.15 Utilizing a highly constrained LoRA rank of 16 and an alpha of 32, they introduced a mere \~7 million trainable parameters per model, vastly reducing the required computational overhead.15 The networks were optimized utilizing the ms-swift framework, employing the AdamW optimizer with a learning rate of ![][image16] over 5 epochs, and leveraging bfloat16 precision to slash the graphical memory footprint by 50%.15

To mitigate the risk of catastrophic overfitting when training on the relatively constrained volume of the DIQA-5000 dataset, NJUST-KMG applied aggressive spatial and radiometric data augmentation during the training phase, including randomized brightness adjustments, nonlinear grid distortions, and randomized cropping.15

The paramount innovation of the NJUST-KMG pipeline was their deployment of a sophisticated Test-Time Augmentation (TTA) strategy.15 Because algorithmic document enhancements often produce highly variable artifacts, algorithmic inference is inherently unstable. To stabilize their predictions, every testing image was passed through the models four distinct times under different deterministic mathematical transformations 15:

1. The unaltered original enhanced image.  
2. A horizontally flipped geometric variant.  
3. A radiometric gamma-corrected variant.  
4. A spatial Gaussian-blurred variant.15

The scalar predictions generated across all four variants were averaged to produce an inherently robust baseline for each individual model.15 Finally, the outputs of the three constituent models were fused using a heavily weighted ensemble strategy to penalize weaker architectures: the superior MiMo-VL-7B model accounted for 40% of the final score, while the Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen2-VL architectures contributed 30% each.15

### **5\. Team GoldenChef (Rank 5 \- Main Score: 0.898)**

Diverging completely from the MLLM consensus that dominated the upper echelons of the leaderboard, Team GoldenChef, led by Mingying Bai, achieved a Main Score of 0.898 utilizing a purely visual, dual-pathway feature extraction framework.2 The team theorized that document quality is a composite of both high-frequency localized textures (such as character edges and algorithmic ink bleed) and low-frequency global layouts (such as macro-illumination variations and geometric page warping).2 Consequently, they engineered an architecture that fused advanced convolutional processing with attention-based transformer networks.2

To handle extreme spatial resolution without invoking catastrophic memory limits or destructive downsampling, their preprocessing pipeline initially resized images to a ![][image17] matrix.2 This matrix was then systematically partitioned into 25 non-overlapping sub-image patches of ![][image18] pixels, which were subsequently randomly cropped to ![][image19] during active training.2

The dual-pathway architecture processed these discrete patches simultaneously:

* **Pathway 1 (ConvNeXt):** Utilized modern ConvNeXt convolutional blocks to extract hierarchical, highly localized textural features, isolating minute distortions like moiré interference patterns and localized defocus blur.2  
* **Pathway 2 (Swin Transformer):** Leveraged shifted-window self-attention mechanisms to model long-range, global contextual representations, identifying broader structural anomalies like physical creases and algorithmic deshadowing failures.2

The highly dimensional feature maps generated by both independent pathways were subsequently concatenated and fused with multi-scale representations. The network branched into separate Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) at the regression head: one specialized MLP independently estimated the subsidiary sharpness and color fidelity metrics, while a distinct, overarching MLP aggregated all feature data to predict the holistic overall quality score.2

### **6\. Team 2077Agent (Rank 6 \- Main Score: 0.828)**

Guided by Fan Yang, Team 2077Agent achieved a Main Score of 0.828 by conceptualizing document quality assessment through the highly experimental lens of generative prior deviation.2 Their architecture, designated the Multi-Expert Feature Fusion Framework with Rectified Flow, sought to quantify optical quality by projecting the degraded images into vast latent diffusion spaces.2

The primary stage of their pipeline utilized a **VAE-based Difference Encoding** mechanism. Relying on the powerful, pre-trained Variational Autoencoder (VAE) native to Stable Diffusion, the team projected the high-resolution document images into a highly compressed, semantically dense latent space, mathematically capturing the granular, pixel-level differences between varied enhancement algorithms.2

These compressed latent representations were subsequently ingested by a multi-expert extraction module containing three parallel neural networks: a Vision Transformer (ViT) dedicated to mapping global attention, a ResNet dedicated to mapping localized textural features, and a MANIQA (Multi-dimension Attention Network for Image Quality Assessment) module explicitly pre-trained for perceptual quality regression.2

To regularize this massive, highly chaotic feature space, 2077Agent introduced a **Rectified Flow** velocity network.2 By applying multi-head attention mechanisms to the fused expert features, the rectified flow acted as a structural regularizer, algorithmically attempting to map the degradation features onto a smooth, predictable mathematical trajectory aimed toward the human MOS values.2 While mathematically sophisticated, the comparative reduction in their Main Score suggests that attempting to map highly specific document legibility metrics onto generative natural-image priors introduces excessive semantic noise into the predictive model.

### **7\. Team BIT ssvgg (Rank 7\)**

Team BIT ssvgg, under the leadership of Ruikun Zhang, implemented a highly sophisticated **Adaptive DIQA Framework** driven by a dynamic Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) system.2 Their methodology compartmentalized the assessment protocol into three distinct temporal stages: initial semantic extraction, adaptive perceptual rule learning, and final scalar quality prediction.2

The input document image was initially processed by a classic ResNet-50 visual encoder to extract foundational spatial and semantic maps.2 However, instead of passing these static feature maps directly into a standard regression head, the features were ingested by a highly scalable MoE HyperNetwork.2 This hypernetwork was designed to adaptively establish unique perceptual rules depending on the localized content of the image. For instance, the routing mechanism would direct text-heavy spatial regions toward expert sub-networks specialized in high-frequency sharpness detection, while simultaneously routing blank background spaces to experts tuned for color fidelity and deshadowing validation.2 These distinct perceptual rules were dynamically weighted and mathematically combined by the hypernetwork to produce the final continuous quality score.2

## **Strategic Insights and Future Technological Trajectories**

The methodologies deployed by the participants in the VQualA 2025 DIQA Challenge illuminate several critical technological trajectories that will irrevocably dictate the future evolution of Document Image Quality Assessment, and computer vision writ large.

The absolute hegemony of the top four teams—all of which abandoned dedicated image quality networks in favor of massively scaled Multimodal Large Language Models—signals a fundamental paradigm shift away from traditional pixel-based regression. The results indicate that evaluating document legibility is inherently a linguistic and semantic concept rather than purely an optical one. Therefore, models pre-trained on vast quantities of text and image pairs possess a vastly superior inductive bias for understanding how specific physical distortions impact reading comprehension. By mathematically translating numerical regression into a cross-modal alignment task (i.e., forcing the model to align a visual embedding with the text "a photo with poor sharpness"), these algorithms leverage the latent reasoning capabilities of language models to parse complex visual degradations.2 The stark failure of older convolutional models like DBCNN to achieve meaningful correlation underscores that shallow structural feature extraction is permanently obsolete for evaluating modern, algorithmically enhanced documents.2

Furthermore, the challenge highlighted that document images present an unparalleled spatial dilemma that breaks conventional deep learning pipelines. Because standard preprocessing irrevocably destroys the precise optical phenomena (like text edge sharpness) that DIQA attempts to measure, future architectures must natively process extreme resolutions. The solutions presented by QA-Veteran utilizing the NaFlex mechanism, and GoldenChef utilizing non-destructive dynamic patching, dictate that future state-of-the-art models must adapt to the document's native aspect ratio without forced geometric compression.2

Equally critical was the field's advancement in probabilistic label engineering. The DIQA-5000 dataset's omission of variance forced teams to abandon treating quality as an absolute scalar. By mathematically synthesizing pseudo-variances based on macroscopic dataset ranges and implementing linear interpolation algorithms, teams successfully mapped deterministic scalars into smoothed Gaussian probability distributions.4 This strategy prevented the massive architectures from overfitting to arbitrary numerical values, instead teaching the models the relativistic distances between perceptual states—proving that modeling uncertainty is mathematically superior to enforcing false precision.

The success of the NJUST-KMG pipeline also establishes Test-Time Augmentation as a stabilizing imperative for DIQA.15 Because algorithmic document enhancements produce highly nonlinear artifacts, forcing the model to reach a mathematical consensus across multiple altered geometric and radiometric states mitigates the risk of hallucinated quality scores, aligning the machine's robust average securely with the true human visual consensus.

The models pioneered on the DIQA-5000 dataset demonstrate that blind perceptual evaluation can now match, and potentially exceed, human expert annotation consistency. By integrating lightweight, LoRA-adapted MLLM variants directly into the front-end of enterprise digitization pipelines, software can instantly quantify sharpness and color fidelity, dynamically routing problematic image patches to specialized, computationally intensive restoration models before attempting text extraction. The techniques refined during the VQualA 2025 challenge establish the definitive technological framework that will govern the development of autonomous, highly reliable document processing and digital archival systems for the foreseeable future.
